slides.title: First, reproduce learning in a simpler setting.
slides.notes: The immediate aim is to reproduce a known language-model learning recipe. Math gives us an answer we can check. Recursive choices come later. This is a small reproduction, not a new method or a reproduction of the paper's headline scores.

slides.title: Reward correct attempts, then change the model.
slides.notes: This example is invented. The model generates its own attempts. The checker supplies only final-answer scores. Relative scores guide weight updates. We use eight attempts per question. If all eight scores agree, there is no within-question learning signal.

slides.title: We train on math, then test on different questions.
slides.notes: Training used chat style. We tested BOTH models with BOTH formats. All 500 questions were excluded from weight training; 64 were monitored. Earlier pretraining exposure is unknown. No worked-solution SFT was added. The original separate 128 test remains 41 to 80.

slides.title: The starting prompt changes the size of the gain.
slides.notes: Read across each row: the prompt stays fixed while weights change. Read down each column: weights stay fixed while the prompt changes. Chat gains 154; question-only gains 12, with 18 gains and six losses. This is one training run, not proof of a general effect.

slides.title: A higher score does not always mean a new skill.
slides.notes: Actual separate-test row 5, summarized. Of its 44 gains, 36 started as capped responses. No generated code was executed. The new run trains with question-only prompts from the original weights. It tests improvement beyond the stronger baseline. Results are pending.
